processing: Little is recorded about this tea on its own; as a Guangdong oolong it would be partly oxidised, rolled into strips and dried.
harvest_season: Not well recorded; Guangdong oolongs are usually picked from spring onward, with spring lots prized.
appearance_dry: Typical of Guangdong oolong: plump, even strips with a brownish, glossy tone.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Guangdong oolong: orange-yellow and clear.
appearance_wet: Typical of strip-style oolong: long leaves that open fully.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting description exists for this name alone; Guangdong oolongs in general lean to natural floral and fruity sweetness.

brewing.notes: General oolong settings; start short and adjust to the leaf in hand.

vintage_note: Nothing specific is recorded about how this name is sold. Oolongs of this type are usually sold as the current year's harvest, so ask for the season and year.
description:
Dabu Wulong simply means oolong from Dabu County in Meizhou, northeastern Guangdong. It appears on lists of Meizhou local products, but little is documented about it as a distinct tea.

The county's best-known oolong is Xi Yan Wulong, from Xiyan Mountain. Whether the Dabu name is a wider label covering that tea and its neighbours is not clear, so read it as a statement of place rather than a defined style.

What you can expect is only what is typical of Guangdong oolong: strip-shaped leaf, an orange-yellow cup, natural floral and fruity sweetness. Brew it as you would any strip oolong, with hot water and short steeps.

When buying, ask who made it and in which part of the county. If the seller can name Xiyan, you can go by what is known of that tea instead.
history: Little is documented about the history of this name. It is known as a Meizhou local product, and the county's oolong became better known through Xi Yan Wulong, created in the late 1970s.
